catalysis-s1.title: Hydrogen peroxide with iodide ions
catalysis-s1.html:
Hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly on its own: 2 H₂O₂(aq) → 2 H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Adding a little potassium iodide makes it fizz quickly. A proposed mechanism:

  1. H₂O₂ + I⁻ → H₂O + IO⁻ (slow)
  2. H₂O₂ + IO⁻ → H₂O + O₂ + I⁻ (fast)

catalysis-s2.title: With and without a catalyst
catalysis-s2.text: Energy profiles for the same reaction by two pathways at the same temperature. Reaction progress has no units.

items.q: In this mechanism, what is the role of I⁻?
options: A catalyst: used in step 1 and remade in step 2
An intermediate: made in step 1 and used in step 2
A reactant: used up as the reaction goes
A product: made in step 2

why.correct: I⁻ is a reactant in step 1 and a product in step 2, so it is consumed and then regenerated, and it does not appear in the overall equation: a catalyst.
options: Right: consumed first, regenerated later.
This is the classic mix-up. An intermediate is made first and then used; I⁻ is used first and then made.
I⁻ is regenerated in step 2, so it is not used up.
I⁻ is also used in step 1, so it is not just a product; it was there at the start.
IO⁻
I⁻
H₂O₂
O₂

why.correct: IO⁻ is made in step 1 and used in step 2, and it was not present at the start.
options: Right: made, then used.
I⁻ is used, then remade: the catalyst.
H₂O₂ is the reactant, used in both steps.
O₂ is a product.

items.q: What rate law does the mechanism predict?
options: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]
rate = k[H₂O₂]²
rate = k[H₂O₂][IO⁻]
rate = k[H₂O₂]

why.correct: The slow first step sets the rate: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]. A catalyst can appear in a rate law, because its concentration is set by the experimenter.
options: Right: from the slow step, catalyst included.
That would match the overall coefficients, which is not how rate laws are found.
IO⁻ is an intermediate and is in the fast step.
I⁻ is a reactant in the slow step, so it must appear.

items.q: A student doubles the amount of KI added (same H₂O₂). Predict each change.

variables.name: Initial rate of O₂ production
variables.why: The rate law includes [I⁻], so doubling it doubles the rate.

variables.name: Total volume of O₂ collected at the end
variables.why: The amount of H₂O₂ sets the amount of O₂; the catalyst is not used up.

variables.name: Amount of I⁻ in solution at the end
variables.why: More I⁻ was added, and all of it is regenerated, so more is present at the end too.

variables.name: Overall energy change of the reaction
variables.why: A catalyst does not change the reactant or product energy levels.

why.correct: More catalyst means more of the fast pathway in use, so a faster rate, but the same amount of product and the same overall energy change.

items.q: A student says, "I⁻ is in the rate law, so it must be a reactant that is used up." Which evidence refutes this?
options: The two steps sum to an equation without I⁻; it is remade
IO⁻ does not appear in the rate law
The reaction fizzes more when KI is added
The rate law is first order in H₂O₂

why.correct: Adding the steps gives 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂; I⁻ cancels because it is used in step 1 and remade in step 2. Being in the rate law only means the slow step involves it.
options: Right: I⁻ cancels from the sum, so it is not consumed.
That is about the intermediate, not about I⁻.
That shows I⁻ speeds the reaction, not whether it is used up.
The order in H₂O₂ says nothing about whether I⁻ is consumed.

items.q: By how much, in kJ/mol, does the catalyst lower the highest point that the reacting particles must pass?

mistakes.why: Value: compare the highest peak on each path: 185 (uncatalyzed) and 135 (catalyzed, second peak), not the first catalyzed peak.
Value: the overall energy change (25 − 60) is the same for both paths; compare the peaks instead.

why.correct: Uncatalyzed peak: 185 kJ/mol. The catalyzed path's highest peak is the second one, at 135 kJ/mol. 185 − 135 = 50 kJ/mol lower.

items.q: Which statement about the two pathways is supported by the graph?
options: Both release 35 kJ/mol; the catalyzed path has two steps
The catalyzed path releases more energy than the uncatalyzed one
The catalyst raises the energy of the products
Both pathways have one step and one transition state

why.correct: Both start at 60 and end at 25 kJ/mol: −35 kJ/mol either way. The catalyzed path has two peaks with a valley between them, so two steps with an intermediate.
options: Right: same start, same end, new two-step path.
Both end at the same product level, so the energy released is the same.
The product level (25 kJ/mol) is the same on both curves.
The catalyzed curve has two peaks, so two steps.

items.q: Why is the catalyzed reaction faster at the same temperature?
options: Its highest barrier is lower, so more collisions succeed
The catalyst gives the molecules extra kinetic energy
The catalyst makes the products more stable
The catalyzed path has more steps, and more steps are faster

why.correct: The catalyst opens a new mechanism whose barriers are lower than the single tall barrier. At the same temperature a larger fraction of collisions has enough energy, so the rate constant is larger.
options: Right: a lower-barrier pathway.
A catalyst does not add energy; the energy distribution depends on temperature.
The product level is unchanged.
More steps do not make a reaction faster; lower barriers do.

items.q: What is the activation energy of the first step of the catalyzed path, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the peak's energy. Subtract the starting level (60 kJ/mol).
Value: that is the second step (135 − 95). The first step climbs from the reactants at 60 to the first peak at 125.

why.correct: First catalyzed step: from the reactants (60) to the first peak (125): 125 − 60 = 65 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which statements about a catalyst are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It is regenerated by the end of the reaction
It changes the energy difference between reactants and products
It raises the kinetic energy of the reacting molecules
It is a reactant that appears in the overall equation

why.correct: A catalyst is consumed in one step and remade in a later one, so it cancels from the overall equation. It changes neither the overall energy change nor the energies of the molecules.
options: Right: not used up overall.
The reactant and product levels are unchanged.
Kinetic energy depends on temperature, not on the catalyst.
A catalyst cancels when the steps are added, so it is not in the overall equation.

items.q: In the mechanism (1) A + Q → AQ; (2) AQ + B → AB + Q, which is the catalyst and which is the intermediate?
options: Catalyst Q; intermediate AQ
Catalyst AQ; intermediate Q
Catalyst B; intermediate AB
Catalyst A; intermediate Q

why.correct: Q is used in step 1 and remade in step 2 (catalyst). AQ is made in step 1 and used in step 2 (intermediate). Overall: A + B → AB.
options: Right: Q first used then remade; AQ first made then used.
Reversed: the catalyst is present at the start, the intermediate is not.
B is a reactant and AB the product.
A is a reactant, used up and never remade.

items.q: In a car's catalytic converter, harmful gases react on the surface of solid platinum. Which statement explains how the metal speeds the reaction?
options: Gas molecules stick to the metal, which weakens their bonds and lowers the barrier
The metal reacts with the gases and is gradually used up
The hot metal gives each molecule enough energy to react
The metal absorbs the products so the reaction can go further

why.correct: This is heterogeneous catalysis: reactant molecules attach to the surface, their bonds weaken, and they react through a lower-energy path. The metal is not used up.
options: Right: a surface pathway with a lower barrier.
A catalyst is regenerated, not consumed (the converter lasts years).
Temperature affects the energy distribution; the catalyst works by lowering the barrier, not by heating.
The products leave the surface; trapping them would block the catalyst.

items.q: A student claims, "A catalyst speeds up only the forward reaction, so it makes more product." Which response is best?
options: It lowers the barrier both ways; the product amount is unchanged
Correct: a catalyst speeds up the forward reaction and gives a higher yield
A catalyst slows the reverse reaction, which is why more product forms
A catalyst speeds up just the reverse reaction

why.correct: Forward and reverse paths share the same transition states, so a lower barrier helps both directions. A catalyst gets the mixture to its final state sooner but does not change how much product forms there.
options: Right: same new path in both directions.
This is the misconception: a catalyst changes rate, not yield.
Lowering the barrier cannot slow the reverse reaction; it speeds it up.
It lowers the barrier for both directions, not one.

items.q: A reaction's activation energy is 132 kJ/mol without a catalyst and 87 kJ/mol with one. By what percentage does the catalyst lower the activation energy?

mistakes.why: Value: divide the drop by the original barrier (132), not by the new one.
Value: that is the new barrier as a percentage of the old one. Subtract it from 100% to get the decrease.

why.correct: Decrease = 132 − 87 = 45 kJ/mol. Percentage = 45/132 × 100% = 34%. The difference, 45, has two significant figures.

items.q: Enzymes are protein catalysts. Why does a small amount of enzyme speed up the reaction of a large amount of reactant?
options: Each enzyme molecule is regenerated and reused many times
Each enzyme molecule reacts with the whole sample at once
The enzyme is used up, but it releases energy as it reacts
The enzyme raises the temperature of the mixture

why.correct: Like any catalyst, an enzyme binds a reactant, helps it react through a lower-barrier path, releases the product and is free to do it again, thousands of times per second.
options: Right: the catalyst is recycled.
An enzyme acts on one or a few reactant molecules at a time.
A catalyst is not used up overall.
Catalysts do not work by heating the mixture.

items.q: Which observation would show that a substance added to a reaction is a catalyst rather than a reactant?
options: Its amount is the same at the end as at the start
The reaction mixture changes color when it is added
It appears in the measured rate law
The reaction gives off more heat when it is added

why.correct: A catalyst is regenerated, so the same amount can be recovered at the end. Appearing in the rate law, a color change, or a change in heat do not by themselves show that a substance is not consumed.
options: Right: recovered unchanged.
A color change can come from an intermediate or a reactant.
Catalysts and reactants can both appear in a rate law.
A catalyst does not change the overall energy released.
